pin_variations.title: Simple Peach Galette with a Buttery Crust—No Fancy Tools Needed
pin_variations.description: Don’t have fancy baking skills? No worries! This peach galette is rustic, simple, and delicious with a buttery crust that’s easy to make. Save this for your next sweet craving! 🍑💛 #easybaking #peachgalette #homemadedessert

ingredients: 8 tablespoons unsalted butter, cold and cubed
introduction: I first fell in love with peach galettes during a summer visit to my aunt’s farmhouse where everything felt slow and sweet. This rustic dessert was always on the table, simple but bursting with peach flavor. Over the years, I’ve tweaked the crust to be extra flaky by keeping the butter cold and using just enough water to bring it together. The secret is not overworking the dough, which keeps it tender and buttery. I also add a little vanilla and cornstarch to the peach filling to keep it juicy but not soggy. What you get is a golden, flaky crust folded casually around sweet, juicy peaches with a light sugar sprinkle that caramelizes perfectly in the oven. It’s a no-fuss dessert that feels homemade and welcoming—ideal for weekend baking when you want something impressive but easy. Plus, it’s just the right balance of crispy and soft, with that fresh peach aroma filling your kitchen. I love how it looks rustic yet tastes like a treat you’d find in a cozy bakery.

instructions.instruction: Combine the flour and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold, cubed butter and use a pastry cutter or your fingers to cut the butter into the flour until the mixture resembles coarse crumbs with some pea-sized bits. This step is crucial because those bits of butter create the flaky layers in the crust when baked. Avoid over-mixing or warming the butter with your hands, as that can make the dough tough.
instructions.doneness_cue: Mixture looks crumbly with small chunks of butter visible—no large butter pieces, no dry flour

instructions.instruction: Add ice water one tablespoon at a time, mixing gently with a fork after each addition until the dough just starts to come together. You want it to hold when pressed but not be sticky. If you add too much water, the dough can become tough. The cold water helps keep the butter firm and creates steam pockets during baking for flakiness.
instructions.doneness_cue: Dough clumps together when pressed but is still slightly crumbly and cool to the touch

instructions.instruction: Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently knead it a few times to bring it fully together. Shape it into a flat disc, wrap in plastic, and chill in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes. Chilling relaxes the gluten and firms the butter again, which helps prevent shrinking and promotes flakiness.
instructions.doneness_cue: Dough feels firm and cold when pressed; no cracks or dryness on surface

instructions.instruction: While the dough chills, prepare the peach filling by tossing sliced peaches with sugar, vanilla extract, and cornstarch in a bowl. The cornstarch absorbs excess juice released during baking, preventing the crust from getting soggy. Let the filling sit for 10 minutes so the flavors meld and the peaches release a bit of juice.
instructions.doneness_cue: Peaches are lightly coated, and mixture looks glossy with slight syrup forming

instructions.instruction: Preheat your oven to 400°F (200°C). On a floured surface, roll out the chilled dough into about a 12-inch circle, roughly 1/8-inch thick. The dough should be even but rustic edges are fine. Transfer it to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Rolling evenly ensures uniform baking and crispness.
instructions.doneness_cue: Dough is thin, round, and smooth with no tears; edges look rustic but intact

instructions.instruction: Mound the peach filling in the center of the dough, leaving a 2-inch border all around. Carefully fold the edges of the dough over the peaches, pleating as needed to enclose the filling partially. This free-form folding creates the classic galette shape while allowing steam to escape.
instructions.doneness_cue: Filling is contained by folded dough edges; pleats look neat but relaxed

instructions.instruction: Brush the exposed dough edges with the beaten egg to give the crust a beautiful golden color when baked. Sprinkle the turbinado sugar over the crust and peaches for a crunchy, sweet finish. This step adds a lovely texture contrast and an attractive shine.
instructions.doneness_cue: Edges are evenly coated with egg wash and sugar crystals are visible

instructions.instruction: Bake the galette in the preheated oven for about 30 minutes, rotating halfway through to ensure even browning. The crust should be golden brown and the filling bubbly but not burnt. Keep an eye towards the end to avoid over-baking which can dry out the crust.
instructions.doneness_cue: Crust is golden and crisp; peach juices bubble and thicken slightly

instructions.instruction: Let the galette cool on the baking sheet for at least 15 minutes before slicing. This resting time lets the juices thicken further and makes it easier to cut clean slices. Serve warm or at room temperature, maybe with a scoop of vanilla ice cream if you like!
instructions.doneness_cue: Galette feels set and firm; juices no longer run freely when cut

why_this_recipe_works.section: Understanding Why This Galette Recipe Works So Well
why_this_recipe_works.content:
The key to a perfect galette lies in the balance between flaky crust and juicy filling. The crust’s flakiness comes from the cold butter cut into the flour just enough to leave pea-sized bits. As the galette bakes, these butter pockets melt and release steam, creating layers that crisp beautifully. Overworking the dough or warming the butter causes gluten to develop too much, making the crust tough instead of tender.

Chilling the dough before rolling it out is essential—it relaxes the gluten strands and firms the butter again. This prevents shrinking during baking and ensures a crisp, tender crust. The ice water helps bind the dough without melting the butter, preserving those flaky pockets.

The peach filling uses cornstarch to absorb excess moisture. Peaches release a lot of juice when baked, which can make the crust soggy if not controlled. Cornstarch thickens the juices, giving a luscious but not runny filling. Adding vanilla enhances the peaches’ natural sweetness and aroma, rounding out the flavor.

Finally, the free-form folding technique of a galette allows steam to escape, preventing sogginess and keeping the crust crispy. Brushing the crust with egg wash and sprinkling sugar adds a golden color and crunchy texture that makes this rustic dessert look as good as it tastes.

ingredient_notes.all-purpose flour: Look for unbleached, all-purpose flour with moderate protein content around 10-11%. This provides enough gluten for a sturdy dough while keeping it tender. Avoid high-protein bread flours as they develop too much gluten, making the crust chewy instead of flaky. Store flour in a cool, dry place to maintain freshness.
ingredient_notes.unsalted butter: Use cold, unsalted butter straight from the fridge. The coldness is crucial for creating flaky layers, and controlling salt lets you adjust seasoning yourself. European-style butters with higher fat content (82-85%) produce richer flavor and flakier crusts. Cut butter into small cubes to chill quickly and prevent melting during mixing.
ingredient_notes.peaches: Choose ripe but firm peaches for the filling to avoid mushy texture. Freestone varieties are easier to slice and have better flavor. If peaches are underripe, add a bit more sugar to compensate. Avoid overly soft or bruised fruit, which will break down too much during baking.
ingredient_notes.cornstarch: This thickener absorbs excess juice released by the fruit during baking. It prevents the crust from becoming soggy and helps the filling set nicely. Use cornstarch rather than flour for a clearer, less pasty filling. Mix it thoroughly with the fruit to avoid clumps.
ingredient_notes.egg (for egg wash): Beaten whole egg brushed on the crust adds a beautiful golden sheen and helps the sugar stick. You can also use just egg yolk for a richer color or egg white for a lighter finish. Fresh eggs provide the best shine and color.

pro_tips.tip: Keep your butter and water very cold while making the dough.
pro_tips.reason: Cold ingredients slow gluten development and keep butter solid, which creates flaky layers during baking. Warm butter melts too soon and results in a dense, tough crust.

pro_tips.tip: Don’t overwork the dough when mixing or kneading.
pro_tips.reason: Overworking develops gluten, making the crust chewy rather than tender. Mix just until the dough comes together to preserve flakiness.

pro_tips.tip: Chill the dough for at least 30 minutes before rolling out.
pro_tips.reason: Resting relaxes gluten strands and firms butter again, preventing shrinking and ensuring a crisp crust.

pro_tips.tip: Use cornstarch to thicken the peach filling.
pro_tips.reason: Cornstarch absorbs excess juice from the peaches, preventing a soggy crust and ensuring the filling sets well.

pro_tips.tip: Roll the dough between two sheets of parchment paper.
pro_tips.reason: This prevents sticking and makes transferring the dough easier without tearing or warming it too much.

pro_tips.tip: Brush the crust edges with egg wash before baking.
pro_tips.reason: Egg wash adds a golden color and helps sugar adhere, creating a beautiful, crunchy finish.

pro_tips.tip: Bake the galette on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
pro_tips.reason: Parchment prevents sticking and makes cleanup easier, while allowing even heat circulation for a crisp crust.

common_mistakes_to_avoid.mistake: Using warm butter or overworking the dough.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.why_it_happens: Many assume more mixing makes dough better, but warm butter melts into the flour and mixing too much develops gluten.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.fix: Keep butter cold and mix just until the dough holds together. Chill the dough before rolling to firm up the butter and relax gluten.

common_mistakes_to_avoid.mistake: Not chilling the dough before baking.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.why_it_happens: Impatience or lack of planning leads to skipping the chill time.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.fix: Always chill dough for at least 30 minutes. This prevents shrinking and creates a flakier crust.

common_mistakes_to_avoid.why_it_happens: Some think sugar alone controls juice, but peaches release a lot of liquid.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.fix: Add cornstarch to absorb juices and keep filling from making the crust soggy.

common_mistakes_to_avoid.mistake: Rolling dough too thin or unevenly.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.why_it_happens: Rushing or lack of technique causes thin spots that can tear or burn.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.fix: Roll evenly to about 1/8 inch thick, using parchment paper to help with smooth rolling.

common_mistakes_to_avoid.mistake: Overbaking and burning the crust or filling.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.why_it_happens: Not watching the oven closely or baking at too high a temperature.
common_mistakes_to_avoid.fix: Bake at 400°F and check at 25 minutes, rotating pan to brown evenly. Remove when crust is golden and filling bubbles.

variations.name: Mixed Berry Galette
variations.description: Swap peaches for a mix of fresh berries like strawberries, blueberries, and raspberries. Adjust sugar slightly depending on berry sweetness. The filling will be juicier and more colorful with a tangy twist.
variations.technical_note: Berries release more juice than peaches, so increase cornstarch to 1.5 tablespoons and bake slightly longer to set filling.

variations.name: Peach and Almond Galette
variations.description: Add sliced almonds to the peach filling and sprinkle some almond extract into the dough. This adds a nutty flavor and crunchy texture that pairs beautifully with the sweet peaches.
variations.technical_note: Toast almonds lightly before adding for extra aroma. Be careful not to overfill or almonds may burn.

variations.name: Gluten-Free Peach Galette
variations.description: Use a gluten-free flour blend instead of all-purpose flour and add a tablespoon of xanthan gum to help bind the dough. The crust will be a bit more delicate but still delicious.
variations.technical_note: Chill dough well and handle gently. Gluten-free dough can be more fragile and may need patching during shaping.

variations.name: Peach and Honey Galette
variations.description: Replace granulated sugar with honey for a floral sweetness and brush some honey on the crust after baking for a glossy finish. The flavor feels more natural and less processed.
variations.technical_note: Honey browns faster, so reduce oven temperature by 25°F and watch closely to prevent burning.

variations.name: Savory Peach Galette with Goat Cheese
variations.description: Add dollops of goat cheese on the peaches and sprinkle fresh thyme before folding. This sweet and savory combo makes an excellent appetizer or brunch item.
variations.technical_note: Bake until crust is golden and cheese is slightly melted but not browned.

storage_and_reheating.room_temperature: Store the galette covered loosely with foil or a cake dome at room temperature for up to 1 day. It’s best served fresh but will keep its texture for a short while without refrigeration.
storage_and_reheating.refrigerator: Keep galette in an airtight container or wrapped tightly with plastic wrap in the fridge for up to 3 days. The crust may soften slightly but reheating in the oven restores crispness nicely.
storage_and_reheating.freezer: Freeze the baked galette wrapped tightly in plastic wrap and aluminum foil for up to 2 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge and reheat in a 350°F oven for 10-15 minutes to crisp the crust.
storage_and_reheating.reheating: Reheat slices in a 350°F oven for 10-15 minutes until warmed through and crust is crisp again. Avoid microwaving as it makes the crust soggy. Add a splash of cream or honey if desired.
storage_and_reheating.make_ahead_strategy: Make the dough and prepare the filling up to 1 day ahead. Store dough chilled and filling refrigerated separately. Assemble and bake just before serving for best texture.

faq.question: Can I use frozen peaches for this galette?
faq.answer: Frozen peaches can work, but thaw and drain them well to remove excess water before using. You may need to add a bit more cornstarch to prevent a soggy crust. Fresh peaches give the best texture and flavor though.

faq.question: What if my dough cracks when rolling it out?
faq.answer: Cracking usually means the dough is too cold or dry. Let it sit at room temperature for a few minutes to soften slightly, then gently press cracks back together. You can also patch cracks with a little water and extra dough.

faq.question: Can I make the galette gluten-free?
faq.answer: Yes! Use a gluten-free flour blend and add xanthan gum to help bind the dough. Handle gently as gluten-free dough can be more fragile. Chill well before rolling out to reduce cracking.

faq.question: How do I prevent the bottom crust from getting soggy?
faq.answer: Using cornstarch in the filling helps absorb juices. Also, rolling the dough to even thickness and baking on a parchment-lined sheet with good oven heat ensures a crisp crust. Avoid overloading the filling with too much fruit.

faq.question: Can I prepare this galette ahead of time?
faq.answer: You can prepare dough and filling up to a day ahead, but it’s best to assemble and bake just before serving. This way, the crust stays flaky and the filling fresh.

faq.question: What’s the best way to slice and serve the galette?
faq.answer: Let the galette cool for at least 15 minutes to let juices thicken. Use a sharp knife and cut into wedges. Serve warm or room temperature, optionally with ice cream or whipped cream.

faq.question: Why is my crust tough instead of flaky?
faq.answer: Likely because the butter melted before baking or the dough was overworked. Keep ingredients cold, mix gently, and chill the dough before rolling to ensure a tender, flaky crust.

faq.question: Can I add spices like cinnamon or nutmeg to the filling?
faq.answer: Absolutely! A pinch of cinnamon or nutmeg complements peaches beautifully. Add about 1/4 teaspoon to the filling for a warm, cozy flavor without overpowering the fruit.

conclusion: I hope you give this peach galette a try and enjoy the flaky crust and juicy peaches as much as I do. Don’t forget to share your baking adventures with friends and family!
